title: Wedgwood's "Am I Not a Man and a Brother?"
text:
In May 1787 a small group in London, most of them Quakers along with Thomas Clarkson and Granville Sharp, founded the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade. They needed to persuade a British public that profited from slavery, and for whom enslaved Africans were mostly out of sight and out of mind.

The committee adopted a seal showing an African man kneeling in chains, hands raised, with the words "Am I Not a Man and a Brother?" Josiah Wedgwood, the great pottery manufacturer and a committee member, had his factory turn the design into small ceramic cameos, black figure on white, and sent them out free by the hundreds.

People began wearing them. Clarkson later wrote that the medallions were set in snuffboxes, bracelets and hairpins, and that ladies wore them as ornaments, so that fashion, usually confined to trivial things, was used in the cause of justice. Wedgwood sent a batch to Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia, who replied that he believed it would be as effective as the best written pamphlet. The image spread on both sides of the Atlantic. Parliament abolished the British slave trade in 1807.
lesson: To change people's minds about how others should be treated, help them see the other as a person like themselves. A simple, human image can persuade where arguments fail.
people: Josiah Wedgwood, Thomas Clarkson, Benjamin Franklin
source: Thomas Clarkson, The History of the Rise, Progress and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave Trade (1808); Benjamin Franklin, letter to Josiah Wedgwood, May 15, 1788
